items.prose: A model of tomorrow's spread on an index future uses 10-day and 30-day moving averages of the spread. Its lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.9. Shuffled 5-fold CV gives an MSE of 1.2; a fit on the first 80% tested on the last 20% gives 2.9.
items.question: Which number should go in the research note?

options.text: 1.2, since cross-validation uses all the data
options.why: Using all the data in shuffled folds is the problem: each test day has its neighbours in training.

options.text: About 2.05, the average of the two
options.why: Averaging keeps half of the leak. Report the honest score.

options.text: Neither: run shuffled CV again with more folds
options.why: More shuffled folds put even more neighbours in training.

feedback.correct: The time-ordered score is the one trading will see.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the score where the model never trains on days near or after the test days.

explain.text: With autocorrelation of 0.9 a shuffled test day has its yesterday and tomorrow in training. Only the time-ordered split matches how the model will be used.

items.question: What is the first row of the last test block?

widget.accept: 400: test blocks are $\lfloor 500/5 \rfloor = 100$ rows and start at 100, 200, 300 and 400.
widget.label: First test row

feedback.correct: Blocks of 100 from row 100: the last starts at 400.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The block size is $\lfloor n/(k+1) \rfloor$.

byKey.first: 100 is where the first test block starts. Count forward to the fourth.
byKey.q: 375 splits 500 into four blocks of 125. `TimeSeriesSplit` uses $k + 1 = 5$ pieces.

explain.text: The first test starts at $500 - 4 \times 100 = 100$, and each block is 100 rows. The fourth runs from 400 to 499.

items.prose: Blocked k-fold with a 10-day forward label and an embargo of 3. The test block sits in the middle of the data.
items.question: How many training rows outside the block do the purge and embargo remove?

widget.accept: 21: $h - 1 = 9$ before, 9 after, and 3 more for the embargo.
widget.label: Rows removed

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count $h - 1$ on each side, then add the embargo.

byKey.one-side: That is the side before the block. In k-fold the rows after it overlap too.
byKey.h: You used $h = 10$ rows per side. A 10-day label overlaps $h - 1 = 9$.
byKey.no-emb: You left out the embargo of 3.

explain.text: Labels over 10 days overlap the test labels for 9 rows on each side. The embargo removes 3 more after the block, for features built from test days.

items.prose: Three walk-forward folds: 100 days with MSE 2.0, 100 days with MSE 2.0, and 40 days with MSE 5.0.
items.question: What is the MSE of the joined out-of-sample predictions?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each fold's MSE by its days.

byKey.mean: You averaged the three MSEs, giving 40 days the weight of 100.

explain.text: Each fold's total squared error is days times MSE: 200, 200 and 200. Over 240 days that is 2.5, not the plain mean of 3.0.

items.prose: You walk forward with `TimeSeriesSplit` on a 5-day forward-return label. The features look back only at past prices.
items.question: Which `gap` removes the label overlap without wasting rows?

options.why: Row $s - 5$ uses days $s - 4$ to $s$, and the first test label starts at $s + 1$. It is clean, so 4 is enough.
The last 4 training rows have labels that use test days.
That throws away 16 clean rows before every block.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count $h - 1$ for a 5-day label.

explain.text: In walk-forward only rows before the block train the model, and the last $h - 1 = 4$ of them overlap. `gap=4` removes exactly those.

items.prose: A signal's five walk-forward folds hit 0.616, 0.600, 0.564, 0.452, 0.424 against a base rate of 0.506. The note says: mean hit rate 53.1%, above the base rate.
items.question: What is the main problem with the note?

options.text: The mean hides that the last two folds, the most recent 500 days, are below the base rate
The edge is too small to matter
options.why: The size is not the main issue. The recent folds are losing, which the mean hides.

options.text: Five folds are too few to compute a mean
options.why: Five is enough to average. The problem is that averaging hides the time pattern.
Using the actual share of up days is right. The problem is the averaging.

feedback.correct: Read folds in time order before averaging.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the order of the fold scores.

explain.text: Folds 4 and 5 lose against the base rate while the first three win. The mean blends them into a number that describes no period at all.

items.prose: A fold of 100 days has hit rate 0.55.
items.question: What is its standard error, $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, using $p = 0.55$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: About 5 points: one 100-day fold is a blunt measure.

byKey.var: That is the variance. Take its square root.

explain.text: $0.55 \times 0.45 = 0.2475$, over 100 is 0.002475, whose root is about 0.0497. A fold at 0.50 would be just one standard error below 0.55.

items.prose: On the same autocorrelated data, shuffled CV flatters a 5-nearest-neighbour model by 2.2 times but a three-coefficient ridge model by only 1.09 times.
items.question: Which model would purging and time order change most, and why?

options.text: The nearest-neighbour model, because it reads predictions straight off the rows closest to the test day
The ridge model, because the penalty interacts with the folds
options.why: The penalty does not look at neighbours. Ridge fits one line through all rows.

options.text: Both equally, since the data are the same
options.why: The data leak equally, but only a model that can memorise rows can use the leak fully.

feedback.correct: Flexible models exploit leaky neighbours most.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which model can copy individual rows.

explain.text: A nearest-neighbour forecast is an average of a few training rows, so leaky neighbours flow straight into it. A rigid line averages over all rows, so the same leak moves it little.
